Inflation heated up last month.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports that's due in part to surging energy prices.
Consumer prices in September were up 3.7% from a year ago.
That's a bigger annual increase than the previous month.
Prices jumped 0.6% between August and September,
with a spike in gasoline prices tied to the U.S. war with Iran,
accounting for more than half that monthly increase.
The cost of rent, airfare, and clothing was also up last month,
while grocery prices were slightly lower.
Stripping out volatile food and energy costs,
core inflation was 2.6% for the 12th month ending in September.
That's also higher than the previous month.
The Federal Reserve will weigh the cost of living data
when officials meet to discuss interest rates in two weeks.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
A federal judge has extended an order blocking the Trump administration
from banning reporters from CNN, MS Now, and Politico from the White House.
The judge says that the ban violates the journalists'
constitutional rights to free speech and due process.
The Justice Department is escalating its threats
to local election jurisdictions as midterms approach.
As NPR's Miles Parks reports,
the DOJ sent a letter of alleged non-citizen voters to LA County this week
and threatened to sue if local officials don't comply with instructions.
The county clerk for LA, Dean Logan,
said the DOJ reached out to his office on Tuesday,
three weeks before Election Day,
with a letter and a USB drive that allegedly included
the names of non-citizens on the county's voter rolls.
In the letter, the department asked Los Angeles to segregate
vote-by-mail ballots returned by the people listed
until their citizenship is confirmed.
Logan says he has not accessed the drive because he couldn't verify it was secure.
But if his office doesn't implement the process requested by the DOJ within 48 hours,
the department says it will sue to compel him to.
That may not be successful.
Judges have dismissed dozens of other DOJ lawsuits during Trump's second term
related to oversight of local election processes.
Miles Parks, NPR News, Washington.
Oregon has paused permitting for new data centers.
It joins two other states with similar data center moratoriums.
Oregon Public Broadcasting's April Ehrlich reports the move also comes as data centers
are proving to be a major issue in the state's governor's race.
Oregon's Democratic Governor Tina Kotek directed the state's environmental regulators
to stop permitting new or expanding data centers until July.
The directive comes amid an unusually tight race for governor
between Kotek and a Republican candidate,
state Senator Christine Drazen.
Oregon hasn't elected a Republican governor since the 1980s.
Each candidate has accused each other of not doing enough
to regulate Oregon's growing data center market.
Amazon is a big player here.
Its executives quickly criticized Kotek's directive as abrupt,
saying it will halt billions of dollars in planned investment.
New York and Texas have similar permitting moratoriums.
For NPR News, I'm April Ehrlich in Portland, Oregon.
Major U.S. stock indexes had their worst day since July today.
This is NPR News from Washington.
Supermarkets in France and the Netherlands
are dealing with the aftermath of a cyber attack that disrupted refrigeration systems.
The attack caused temperatures to soar, leading to significant food losses.
Investigations are underway, but no perpetrators have been identified.
Experts say the attack highlights vulnerabilities in older refrigeration systems
and the need for better cybersecurity measures.
More than 9,000 people have gotten sick during the ongoing Ebola outbreak,
according to health officials.
As NPR's Jonathan Lambert reports, cases are popping up outside the epicenter.
Democratic Republic of Congo officials confirmed that there have been 9,144 cases
and over 4,400 deaths, making this the second largest Ebola outbreak ever.
Early hotspots of spread have slowed down a bit,
but the virus has moved into new territory.
The province of North Kivu is particularly affected,
and ongoing conflict there is slowing response efforts.
Over 70 percent of deaths are still occurring outside of treatment centers.
That suggests efforts to monitor potential cases
and get them to seek treatment are falling short.
The virus is also spreading outside of DRC.
Last week, Kenya reported its first case in a man who traveled home from DRC.
Now, one of his family members has gotten sick.
Kenyan health officials said this second case was already in quarantine
and is now being treated.
Jonathan Lambert, NPR News.
New York City is moving toward a ban
on the more than 150-year-old horse-drawn carriage industry
following the death of a teenage tourist in Central Park.
The city council is expected to approve a bill next week
that would shutter the practice by 2028.
Mayor Zaraan Mamdani said on X that the industry is coming to an end in the city.
This is NPR News.
